predict: If a website gets only 400 visitors a week, do you think it can run a useful A/B test? Guess why or why not.

quiz.q: Your landing page converts at 4% and gets 6,000 sessions a week. You want to detect a 10 percent relative lift (4.0% to 4.4%) at 95% confidence and 80% power, using n per variant of roughly 16 x p x (1 - p) divided by the absolute MDE squared. What does the calculation say?
options: About 3,840 sessions per variant, roughly a week and a half of traffic.
About 19,200 sessions per variant, roughly six weeks of traffic.
About 38,400 sessions per variant, roughly thirteen weeks of total traffic.
About 153,000 sessions per variant, roughly fifty weeks of traffic.
quiz.why: The absolute MDE is 0.004, so n is 16 x 0.04 x 0.96 divided by 0.000016, about 38,400 per variant and roughly 77,000 sessions in total, or about thirteen weeks at 6,000 a week. The tempting error is using the relative 10% figure as the MDE, which gives an absurdly small 3,840 and makes an unfeasible test look like a week's work.

quiz.q: You planned a test at a 20 percent MDE needing about 26,000 sessions in total. Your CMO asks you to make it sensitive enough to catch a 10 percent lift instead. What happens to the traffic requirement?
options: It roughly quadruples, to about 103,000 sessions.
It roughly doubles, to about 52,000 sessions.
It is unchanged; MDE affects only how wide the confidence interval ends up being.
It roughly halves, because a smaller effect is easier to reach significance on.
quiz.why: Sample size scales with one over the MDE squared, so halving the effect you want to detect quadruples the traffic required. Doubling feels intuitive because the effect halved, but the relationship is quadratic, and this single fact should govern testing strategy on modest traffic.

quiz.q: A test was planned for four weeks and 40,000 sessions. On day nine the variant is at plus 12 percent with p = 0.04, and the head of growth wants to ship it now. What is the right call?
options: Ship it. A p-value of 0.04 is below 0.05, so the result is valid whenever you looked at it.
Ship it, then re-run the same test on the other half of traffic to confirm.
Stop and rebuild it as a multivariate test to find which element drove the lift.
Keep it running to the pre-committed sample size and at least two whole weeks, then look once and decide.
quiz.why: The significance maths assumes one look at a pre-committed sample size; under repeated daily looks a null test will eventually cross 95% by chance, which is how marketers manufacture false wins. Shipping because 0.04 is below 0.05 ignores that the threshold was reached during peeking, not at the planned horizon.

quiz.q: A test reports a 15 percent lift with p = 0.09 and a 95% confidence interval running from minus 3 percent to plus 33 percent. What should you conclude?
options: There is a 9 percent chance the variant is better than the control.
The data are consistent with anything from a small loss to a large gain, so this is worth pursuing rather than filing as no difference.
The variant has been shown to make no difference, so drop the idea.
The effect is real but too small to be commercially interesting.
quiz.why: The interval is the honest report: probably positive, possibly nothing, worth another look. Absence of significance is not evidence of no difference and usually means the test was too small, so treating p = 0.09 as proof the variant does nothing throws away a potentially valuable finding.

quiz.q: You ran a checkout test with conversion rate as the pre-registered primary metric and refund rate and AOV as named guardrails. Conversion is up 8 percent and significant, refunds are up 20 percent, and AOV is up 3 percent but not significant. What do you do?
options: Ship it. Conversion was the primary metric and it won.
Ship it and lead the report with the AOV improvement.
Record it as a loss, investigate the refunds, and do not ship until you understand them.
Re-analyse with AOV as the primary metric, since AOV is closer to money.
quiz.why: A guardrail is a thing that must not get worse, and a conversion lift bought with a 20 percent rise in refunds is a loss for the business. Shipping on the primary metric alone is the common error, and switching the primary metric after the fact is exactly how organisations accumulate confident falsehoods.

quiz.q: Your business produces about 300 conversions a month and the team wants to build an A/B testing programme. What is the senior response?
options: Below roughly 1,000 conversions a month almost nothing but a very large effect is detectable, so use bigger swings, painted-door tests, five user interviews and best-practice priors, and write down the reasoning.
Run the tests anyway at 90 percent confidence instead of 95 percent to compensate for the low volume.
Run tests for six months each so the sample accumulates to a valid size.
Switch to multivariate testing so each visitor contributes information about several elements at once.
quiz.why: Saying you lack the traffic, deciding on evidence and judgment, and stating what would change your mind is the senior answer; running the test anyway and reporting a fake 95 percent is the junior one. Multivariate is the worst option here because required traffic multiplies by the number of cells.

cards.front: What are the four parts of a usable hypothesis?
cards.back: Because [evidence], we expect [specific change] to cause [effect on one metric], measured by [metric, over what period]. The because is the part that matters, and it tells you what to do when the test loses.

cards.front: What happens to required sample size when you halve the effect you want to detect?
cards.back: It roughly quadruples, because sample size scales with one over MDE squared. On modest traffic this means only testing changes big enough to produce big effects.

cards.front: Why are before-after comparisons usually invalid, and when are they acceptable?
cards.back: They measure your change plus the world: weekday mix, seasonality, competitor promotions, press. Acceptable only for unsplittable changes such as a rebrand or price change, with a long baseline, an explicit non-causal note and ideally a geographic control.

cards.front: What does peeking do to a test, and what does a stopping rule contain?
cards.back: Repeated looks let a null test eventually cross 95 percent by chance. The rule fixes the sample size, whole business cycles rather than partial weeks, and one look at the end.

cards.front: You have 400 sessions a week. Name four substitutes for A/B testing.
cards.back: Bigger swings in offer, page or positioning; painted-door and smoke tests; five user tests or customer interviews; best-practice priors; account-level holdouts for ads.

cards.front: What does a p-value of 0.04 mean, and what does it not mean?
cards.back: If the variant made no difference, a gap this large would arise by chance 4 percent of the time. It is not the probability the variant is better, and it says nothing about effect size.

elaborate: Take the single biggest change you would like to make to your chosen business's main page. Write it as a four-part hypothesis grounded in a specific piece of evidence you can name, then compute the sample size for a 10 percent and a 25 percent relative lift using your real baseline rate and weekly traffic. Conclude honestly whether you can test it at all.

M13 argued that no measurement method is true. Explain in your own words why a randomised test is the exception, then name one decision in your chosen business you will have to make on judgment because the test is not feasible, and write down exactly what evidence would change your mind.

transfer.scenario: A direct-to-consumer skincare brand gets 5,000 sessions a week and converts at 2.5 percent. The founder wants to test a new homepage hero image and thinks it might produce a 5 percent relative lift. She has generated 40 hero variants with AI, plans to run them all this month, check the dashboard every morning, and ship the first one that crosses 95 percent confidence.
transfer.prompt: Tell her what the sample size arithmetic says about this plan, and what you would do with the month instead.
transfer.model: The arithmetic kills the plan. At a 2.5 percent baseline and a 5 percent relative lift the absolute MDE is 0.00125, so n is about 16 x 0.025 x 0.975 divided by 0.00125 squared, roughly 250,000 sessions per variant, half a million in total, or around two years at 5,000 sessions a week. Forty variants make it worse, not better, and shipping the first to cross 95 percent while checking daily manufactures a winner out of noise. So do not run it. Spend the month on a bolder swing, a different offer or hero proposition rather than an image, plus five user tests and a painted-door test for the product she has not built. Put the AI variants where volume actually exists, in the ad account. Record the decision and the evidence that would change it in the test log.

predict: Your ad report says the ads on your own brand name deliver your cheapest cost per sale. Guess one reason that number might be misleading.

quiz.q: A channel returns £27,000 of revenue at £6,000 of monthly spend and £29,500 at £8,000. Your gross margin is 40 percent, so break-even ROAS is 2.5x. Do you keep the last £2,000?
options: Yes. Average ROAS at £8,000 is 3.7x, comfortably above break-even.
No. The last £2,000 returned £2,500, a marginal 1.25x, well below the 2.5x break-even.
Yes. Total revenue still rose, so the increment added money to the business.
You cannot tell without an MMM, because marginal return is not observable.
quiz.why: Allocation decisions are made on marginal return, not average. The 3.7x average includes the first, cheapest, most incremental pounds, so it hides the fact that the last increment lost money on margin; and you approximate marginal return by stepping spend up and down and watching, not by commissioning a model.

quiz.q: Branded search takes £3,000 a month and reports 400 conversions, a £7.50 CPA that looks like the best line in the account. A four-week geo holdout pauses it and conversions in the holdout regions fall 12 percent, not 100 percent. What follows?
options: About 48 conversions were incremental, so the true incremental CPA is around £62.50 and keeping it becomes an insurance decision at a known price.
About 352 conversions were incremental, so the CPA is around £8.50 and nothing changes.
The holdout proves branded search is worthless and it should be switched off.
A 12 percent drop is within noise, so the reported £7.50 CPA stands.
quiz.why: Twelve percent of 400 is about 48 incremental conversions, so £3,000 divided by 48 is roughly £62.50, an entirely different decision from £7.50. Switching it off does not follow: competitors bidding on your name, control of message and sitelinks, and marketplaces outranking you are defensible reasons to keep buying it, now priced honestly.

quiz.q: MMM, incrementality tests and platform attribution disagree about a channel. How should you rank your confidence?
options: Platform attribution first, because it is closest to the daily decisions and updates fastest.
MMM first, because it sees the whole portfolio including offline.
Independent incrementality testing first, MMM second, in-platform reporting last.
All three equally, averaging their estimates to get a balanced view.
quiz.why: Senior decision-makers trust independent incrementality testing most, MMM second and in-platform reporting least, because platform attribution systematically over-claims. MMM sounds like the most authoritative choice, but it is not tactical and overfits easily; when the three disagree, that disagreement tells you where to run the next test.

quiz.q: An ecommerce business has two years of weekly data and has spent almost exactly £5,000 on Meta and £3,000 on Google every single week throughout. It wants to commission an MMM. What do you tell them?
options: Two years of weekly data clears the bar, so the model will work.
Meridian or Robyn will handle it, because open-source models cope with thin variation.
It will work for the online channels but not for anything offline.
It will learn very little, because MMM needs real variation in spend by channel and identical weekly spend gives the model nothing to separate.
quiz.why: MMM needs two to three years of weekly data, real variation in spend by channel, and clean records of promotions and price changes; spend identically every week and it learns nothing. The data-length requirement is met here, which is why this case is tempting, but no software fixes missing variation, and judging an MMM on how good the numbers look rather than whether spend varied is a listed mistake.

quiz.q: You are about to move £4,500 out of retargeting and branded search into Meta prospecting, creative production and brand video. What must you tell the CFO before you do it?
options: That reported total ROAS should rise within four weeks as the money goes to better channels.
That reported total ROAS will fall by construction, and that the decision will be judged on total revenue and blended CAC over eight weeks.
That you will judge each destination channel on its own reported ROAS from now on.
That attribution will become more accurate once the flattering channels are smaller.
quiz.why: Reported ROAS falls because you moved money out of the channels best at claiming credit; if you cannot explain that in advance you will be blamed for the dashboard. Blended CAC, total spend divided by all new customers, is the check that cannot be gamed by reallocating credit.

quiz.q: A consumer brand has flat sales volume, rising CPAs and falling branded search volume. The growth lead proposes cutting all brand video to fund more non-brand search. What is the judgment?
options: Correct. Brand spend has no measurable ROAS, so it should be the first line cut.
Correct. The 60/40 heuristic applies only to large established brands, so activation should take everything.
Wrong. Rising CPAs at flat volume with falling branded search suggest the demand pool is shrinking, which argues for shifting toward brand, not away from it.
Neither. Freeze the budget at a percentage of revenue until CPAs stabilise.
quiz.why: Branded search volume and direct traffic are the proxy for the size of the demand pool; flat or falling while you push harder on capture means you are harvesting a shrinking field. This is the named failure pattern - cut creation, then blame the market for the two-quarter decline - and the 60/40 split shifts toward brand when CPAs climb at flat volume.

cards.front: Why does scaling the channel with the best reported return fail?
cards.back: It reasons from average ROAS, which includes the first and most incremental pounds. Correct allocation equalises marginal return across channels, and marginal return only becomes visible through holdouts.

cards.front: What is an incremental conversion, and name three ways to measure incrementality?
cards.back: One that would not have happened without the ad. Geo holdouts, PSA or ghost ads, platform conversion lift studies, and switch-back tests, which are cheap but weak.

cards.front: Where does non-incremental spend hide, and why?
cards.back: Branded search and retargeting. Both advertise to people already coming: one typed your name, the other already visited. They produce the most flattering reported numbers in the account, so test them first.

cards.front: What does MMM need, and name one thing it is good at and one it is bad at?
cards.back: Two to three years of weekly data, real variation in spend by channel, clean promotion and price records. Good at the portfolio view including offline and long-term effects; bad at tactical questions, correlated channels and small businesses.

cards.front: Which budget-setting method survives a hostile question, and why?
cards.back: Objective-and-task. State the objective, enumerate the tasks, cost each, sum. Every line traces to a named assumption you can revise. Sanity-check against percent of revenue and competitive parity, then set a floor and ceiling.

cards.front: What are the three legs of triangulation and what does each answer?
cards.back: MMM: how the whole portfolio contributes, quarterly. Incrementality tests: is this spend causing anything, a few per year. Platform attribution: what to change now, daily, and it over-claims systematically.

elaborate: Pick the most flattering line in your chosen business's ad account, the one with the best reported return. Design the cheapest holdout that could test it: which slice, how many weeks, what you will measure from your own records rather than the platform's, what result would change your allocation, and what it costs in forgone sales.

M14 argued you probably lack the traffic for a valid A/B test. Explain why a geo holdout can still be a workable method for the same business, and what M14's power argument implies about running a holdout on a slice that produces 30 conversions a month.

transfer.scenario: An ecommerce account spends £25,000 a month at 55 percent gross margin, so break-even ROAS is about 1.8x. Retargeting takes £5,000 at a reported 7.0x with no holdout ever run. Non-brand search takes £12,000 at a reported 3.0x, with marginal ROAS on the last £3,000 measured at 1.9x, and Meta prospecting takes £6,000 at a reported 1.6x with a May geo holdout showing real lift. Creative production takes the remaining £2,000. The CEO wants to move £3,000 out of Meta prospecting into retargeting because retargeting is the best channel.
transfer.prompt: Decide whether to make the move, and write what you would say to the CEO.
transfer.model: I would not make that move. Retargeting's 7.0x is reported, not incremental, and it advertises to people who already visited, which is exactly where non-incremental spend hides. Before any money moves toward it, run a four-week holdout in one matched region. If it returns 30 percent incremental, a common result, its true return is about 2.1x against a 1.8x break-even, barely worth the spend, and money should be leaving it rather than arriving. Meta prospecting is the only line with holdout evidence of real lift, and non-brand search is already at 1.9x on its last £3,000, so it cannot absorb more either. I would tell the CEO in advance that if we reallocate correctly the reported total ROAS will fall by construction, and that we will judge the decision on total revenue and blended CAC over eight weeks.

predict: A B2B software company generates 300 leads a month and the sales team says they are all rubbish. Guess what is most likely wrong.

quiz.q: Target £3,000,000 of new ARR at a £30,000 average contract value. Observed rates: 25 percent of opportunities close, 50 percent of SQLs become opportunities, 25 percent of MQLs become SQLs. How many MQLs per month does the plan need?
options: About 267.
About 133.
About 67.
About 800.
quiz.why: £3m at £30k is 100 customers; at a 25 percent win rate that is 400 opportunities, at 50 percent that is 800 SQLs, at 25 percent that is 3,200 MQLs a year, about 267 a month. The 133 answer comes from dropping one stage of the chain, which is the most common arithmetic slip in pipeline modelling.

quiz.q: That same plan needs 400 opportunities a year. The company has four sales reps, each of whom works about 60 opportunities a year. What should the marketer say in the planning meeting?
options: Nothing yet. Reps typically work harder in the fourth quarter.
Nothing. Marketing owns MQLs, so a queue of unworked leads is a sales problem.
Capacity is 240 opportunities against 400 needed, so the target is unreachable without roughly three more reps or a lower target, and saying so now is the valuable move.
Raise the MQL target further to compensate for the low win rate.
quiz.why: Without the capacity check, 2,700 or 3,200 MQLs produce a queue and a lead-quality argument rather than revenue. Raising MQL volume is the tempting answer because it is the lever marketing controls, but it makes the bottleneck worse, and stating the arithmetic early is described as the most valuable thing a marketer does in annual planning.

quiz.q: A CEO wants to cut a LinkedIn thought-leadership programme because it produces very few MQLs per pound. What is the strongest response?
options: Agree. If it does not produce MQLs at an acceptable cost it is not working.
Gate it, so it starts producing MQLs and can be measured on the same basis.
Keep it but move its budget into retargeting so the clicks convert.

Most of the audience cannot buy now, so response metrics structurally undervalue the work; judge it on branded search volume, direct traffic, how-did-you-hear-about-us share and inbound requests naming you, plus pipeline over quarters.
quiz.why: The 95-5 rule says only a small share of buyers are in-market at any moment, so advertising that reaches the rest is memory-building, not waste, and the 95 percent cannot respond to a response metric. Gating it is the seductive wrong answer: it makes the programme measurable by suppressing exactly the reach that was doing the work.

quiz.q: You have two assets ready: an ROI calculator and an essay on where the category is heading. What is the mature gating decision?
options: Gate both. Every asset should earn contact details.
Gate the ROI calculator, which carries real buying signal, and ungate the essay, whose value is reach and memory.
Ungate both. Gating always degrades lead quality.
Gate the essay, since it is the more valuable content, and ungate the calculator as a free tool.
quiz.why: Gate things carrying genuine buying signal - ROI calculators, benchmark tools, pricing guides, assessments - and ungate thought leadership whose value is reach. Never gating is not the position either; the failure of gated lead gen is gating curiosity, which fills the CRM with people who downloaded a PDF.

quiz.q: Sales says lead quality is bad. Marketing says sales does not work the leads. Which single element of an SLA settles the argument?
options: A higher MQL scoring threshold, so fewer and better leads are handed over.
A monthly MQL volume commitment from marketing.
Mandatory disposition of every lead in the CRM with a reason code, reviewed jointly each month.
A four-business-hour first-response commitment from sales.
quiz.why: Reason codes turn lead quality from an opinion into a measurable: you can see it is 40 percent wrong-company-size and fix the targeting. The response-time commitment is a real and important part of the SLA and materially changes contact rates, but it does not tell you why leads were rejected.

quiz.q: Your Performance Max campaign is being fed form fill as its conversion event, and the resulting leads are mostly unqualified. What is the highest-leverage fix?
options: Add negative keywords and tighten the audience signals so the algorithm looks at better people.
Import SQLs and closed-won deals with values back from the CRM as offline conversions, so the algorithm optimises toward revenue rather than forms.
Move the budget to manual campaigns where you control targeting directly.
Raise the form's friction by adding qualifying questions until volume falls.
quiz.why: Black-box platforms optimise toward whatever conversion you feed them, so feed form fill and they find the cheapest form-fillers alive; the offline conversion feed is described as the highest-leverage technical task in B2B paid media. Tightening targeting is the instinctive answer, but with Performance Max the algorithm, not you, allocates to keywords and placements.

cards.front: Name four buying committee roles and the question each asks.
cards.back: Economic buyer: what is the return and the risk to me. Champion or user: does this improve my work and can I sell it internally. Technical evaluator: does it integrate and is it secure. Procurement: price, terms, contract risk.

cards.front: What is the most common outcome of a B2B deal, and what does that imply?
cards.back: No decision. Committees default to inaction because inaction is safe, so you must differentiate against doing nothing as well as against competitors, and supply risk-reduction material for consensus.

cards.front: State the 95-5 rule and its two implications.
cards.back: Only around 5 percent of potential buyers are in-market at any moment. So most advertising reaches people who cannot buy, which is memory rather than waste, and response-rate metrics systematically undervalue that work.

cards.front: What does the SAL stage exist for?
cards.back: Sales Accepted Lead exists purely to make rejection visible and measurable. Without it you cannot see what sales refused to work or why, and lead quality stays an argument instead of a number.

cards.front: When is ABM worth it, and when is it not?
cards.back: Worth it for large deals, roughly six figures up, an enumerable market, complex committees and real sales coordination. Not for low-value, high-volume, self-serve products. Metrics become account engagement, meetings and in-list pipeline.

cards.front: What is the practical attribution stance for long B2B cycles?
cards.back: Track touchpoints at contact and account level in the CRM, treat multi-touch reporting as directional only, lean harder on self-reported attribution, judge demand creation on pipeline over quarters, and run holdouts by geography, industry or account tier.

elaborate: Map the buying committee for your chosen business, or for a plausible B2B version of it if it is B2C: every role, the one question each asks, and the single asset that answers it. Mark the likeliest blocker and say exactly what you would put in your champion's hands to win the internal argument you will never attend.

Run the pipeline math backwards from a revenue target using your real or best-estimated rates, then apply the two constraints people forget, sales capacity and cycle length. State whether the target is achievable and what specifically would have to change - and connect this to M15's point that only objective-and-task budgeting survives a hostile question.

transfer.scenario: A B2B SaaS company has been given a target of £1,600,000 in new ARR next year at a £16,000 average contract value. Observed rates: 20 percent of opportunities close, 50 percent of SQLs become opportunities, 20 percent of MQLs become SQLs. Blended cost per MQL is £200. The company has three sales reps who each work about 60 opportunities a year, and the average sales cycle is five months. The CMO has been given a £600,000 budget.
transfer.prompt: Say whether the target is achievable, and write what you would tell the CEO in the planning meeting.
transfer.model: The target is not achievable, and I would say so with the arithmetic in front of me. £1.6m at £16,000 is 100 customers; at a 20 percent win rate that is 500 opportunities, 1,000 SQLs and 5,000 MQLs, about 417 a month. Three things break it. Cost: 5,000 MQLs at £200 is £1,000,000 against a £600,000 budget. Capacity: three reps at 60 opportunities each is 180, not 500, so most of the pipeline sits untouched and we get a lead-quality argument instead of revenue. Cycle: a five-month average means anything generated after month seven cannot close this year, so the plan must be front-loaded. On current headcount and budget the defensible sourced number is around £600,000. To move it, we need reps hired now, a tighter MQL definition to lift the 20 percent MQL-to-SQL rate, and offline conversion imports so the ad platforms optimise toward SQLs.

predict: Two subscription businesses have identical products and prices, but one loses 3 percent of customers a month and the other loses 8 percent. Guess one advantage the first has when both bid on the same ad.

quiz.q: A £60 per month subscription has a 55 percent gross margin and 6 percent monthly churn. At a 3:1 LTV:CAC target, what is the most you can pay to acquire a customer?
options: About £183.
About £333.
About £550.
About £110.
quiz.why: Lifetime is 1 divided by 0.06, about 16.7 months; LTV on gross profit is £60 x 0.55 x 16.7, about £550; at 3:1 that is roughly £183. The £333 answer computes LTV on revenue rather than gross profit, which is the listed mistake that leads companies to over-spend on a number around 40 percent too high.

quiz.q: That same business cuts churn from 6 percent to 4.5 percent, a 25 percent relative improvement. What happens to lifetime and max CAC?
options: Lifetime rises about 25 percent, to roughly 21 months, and max CAC rises about 25 percent to £229.
Lifetime is unchanged; only payback improves, because customers pay for longer.
Lifetime rises to about 22.2 months, LTV to about £733, and max CAC to about £244.
Lifetime rises to about 18 months and max CAC to about £198.
quiz.why: 1 divided by 0.045 is 22.2 months, so LTV is £33 of monthly gross profit times 22.2, about £733, and max CAC at 3:1 is about £244 - a 33 percent rise in acquisition power from a 25 percent churn improvement. Assuming lifetime moves in proportion to the churn cut misses that the relationship is reciprocal, not linear.

quiz.q: Your cohort table shows month-6 retention of 34, 33, 35 and 36 percent across four consecutive cohorts, with each curve dropping steeply then levelling from about month four. What is the right reading?
options: Losing 65 percent of customers by month six means retention is the emergency to fix before anything else.
The curve flattens around 35 percent, so there is a durable core; growth compounds on top of that plateau, and later cohorts are holding or slightly improving.
Report the average retention rate across all customers to the board, as it is the cleanest summary.
Later cohorts are worse, which suggests a channel change brought in poorer customers.
quiz.why: A curve that drops then levels means a durable core genuinely needs the product, and that plateau is the real business; a curve declining toward zero is the emergency. Averaging across all customers is explicitly wrong because a growing company's average is dominated by new joiners and hides every trend that matters.

quiz.q: Analysis shows customers who invite a teammate in week one retain at twice the rate of those who do not. The product team proposes forcing everyone through a mandatory invite step. What is the judgment?
options: Do it. A doubling is a strong enough signal to act on immediately.
Do it, and measure the result with a before-after comparison of the next two months.
Use inviting as a lagging indicator in the board pack instead of a leading one.
Test whether it is causal first. If inviting is a symptom of already-motivated users, pushing everyone toward it changes nothing.
quiz.why: An activation metric must be causally plausible, not merely correlated; chasing a correlated metric and pushing users toward a behaviour that never caused anything is a listed mistake. The before-after option is doubly wrong, since M14 established that before-after comparisons measure your change plus everything else that happened.

quiz.q: Your content loop runs: publish, rank or get shared, attract users, users leave reviews and questions, that becomes more publishable material. What have you built?
options: A network effect, since more users make the content better for everyone.
A viral loop, correctly measured by the viral coefficient k.
A growth loop but not a network effect: it makes you bigger, not more useful per user, so it creates efficiency rather than defensibility.
A paid loop, whose speed limit is the payback period.
quiz.why: A loop is a growth mechanism where output feeds input; a network effect is a value mechanism where the product gets better for each user as more join. Calling a loop a network effect is a named mistake, and the distinction matters because network effects create defensibility while loops only create efficiency.

quiz.q: A wedding venue owner asks whether to redirect budget from acquisition into churn reduction, having read that retention beats acquisition. What do you tell her?
options: For a genuinely one-off high-ticket purchase, acquisition remains the main engine, and retention is redefined as referrals, reviews, reputation and adjacent services.
Retention beats acquisition almost always, so redirect the budget and build a loyalty programme.
Compute LTV projected to infinity first, since a venue's brand lasts decades.
Launch a referral programme with a cash bounty to compensate for the lack of repeat purchase.
quiz.why: Retention wins for subscription and repeat-purchase businesses, but nobody buys a second loft conversion, and the module names one-off high-ticket purchases as the exception. A cash bounty is the wrong reward too: it attracts people who want cash and produces customers who churn.

cards.front: Why does a churn improvement raise the CAC you can afford?
cards.back: Lifetime is one over churn, so lower churn lengthens lifetime and raises LTV on gross profit. At a fixed LTV:CAC ratio a higher LTV means a higher max CAC, letting you outbid competitors for the same click.

cards.front: Logo churn versus revenue churn, and what does NRR above 100 percent mean?
cards.back: Logo churn counts customers lost, revenue churn counts money lost, and the gap shows which customers you are losing. NRR above 100 percent means expansion outgrows churn, so the base grows while acquiring nobody.

cards.front: What does a flattening cohort curve tell you, and a non-flattening one?
cards.back: Flattening means a durable core genuinely needs the product and growth compounds on that plateau. Declining toward zero means no core exists, so you must acquire forever, faster, just to stand still.

cards.front: Time-to-value, activation metric, and the trap in choosing one.
cards.back: Time-to-value is elapsed time from signup to first real benefit. The activation metric is the observable early behaviour that predicts retention. The trap is picking a symptom of already-motivated users rather than a causal behaviour.

cards.front: Name four growth loops with an example each.
cards.back: Viral: invites inside a collaboration tool. Content: reviews and questions becoming publishable pages. Paid: margin funding the next acquisition, limited by payback. UGC: customers posting after delivery. B2B word of mouth: a reference shortening the next deal.

cards.front: What makes a referral programme actually work?
cards.back: A product worth talking about, a double-sided reward so sharing is a favour, credit rather than cash, asked at the moment of realised value, frictionless mechanics, and measured on retained referred customers rather than shares.

elaborate: Compute the whole chain for your chosen business: churn or repeat rate, average lifetime, LTV on gross profit at a capped horizon, max CAC at your chosen ratio, and payback. Recompute it with a 25 percent relative churn improvement and name the specific channels the new max CAC would make affordable that are closed to you today.

M15 said the right allocation equalises marginal return across channels. Using your own numbers, argue in three sentences whether a 20 percent churn improvement or 20 percent more acquisition spend is worth more next quarter, and state what would have to be true for the answer to flip.

transfer.scenario: A £39 per month B2B tool has a 70 percent gross margin, 9 percent monthly churn and a CAC of £190. Cohort analysis shows 45 percent of churn happens in the first 45 days, and customers who import their data in week one retain at roughly twice the rate; the current week-one import rate is 31 percent. The founder wants to put an extra £8,000 a month into Google Ads rather than fix onboarding, because ads produce customers this quarter and onboarding work does not.
transfer.prompt: Decide where the £8,000 goes, and justify it with the arithmetic.
transfer.model: Fix onboarding first. Today lifetime is 1 divided by 0.09, about 11.1 months; monthly gross profit is £27.30, so LTV is roughly £303 against a £190 CAC. That is 1.6:1 with a seven-month payback, so an extra £8,000 buys about 42 customers a month at a ratio that barely works. The cohort data points at the real lever: 45 percent of churn lands in the first 45 days, and week-one data import roughly doubles retention at only a 31 percent import rate. Test whether importing is causal rather than a symptom of motivated users, then move it into signup, add a one-click path and a day-two nudge. If churn falls from 9 to 6.5 percent, lifetime reaches 15.4 months and LTV about £420, a 39 percent gain that every future cohort inherits and that raises the CAC we can afford. No ad optimisation compounds like that.

predict: If AI can write a hundred articles a week for almost nothing, guess why that might make a company's marketing worse rather than better.

quiz.q: In an Advantage+ and Performance Max world where the algorithm allocates to keywords and placements, which use of AI is the clearest return in paid media?
options: Publishing 40 SEO articles a month so the algorithm has more landing pages to work with.
Letting the model decide the budget split between campaigns each week.
Creative variant production: ten headline angles, six hooks, five image concepts for one offer.
Generating the audience segments the platform should target.
quiz.why: Creative volume and diversity is the main input you still control when buying is automated, which makes variant production the clearest ROI use in paid media. Audience generation is the tempting wrong answer because it feels like the sophisticated task, but targeting is precisely the part the black box has taken over.

quiz.q: A B2B company has published 120 AI-written articles restating what already sits on page one. Traffic is flat and demo requests are unchanged. What is the diagnosis?
options: Publish more; volume compounds once there is enough of it to be picked up in AI Overviews.
The prompts are the problem; better prompts would make the same articles rank.
Gate the articles so at least they produce leads while the traffic builds.

With around 60 percent of searches ending click-free, the marginal generic article earns close to nothing; what answer engines have reason to cite is original research and first-hand data, which is exactly what AI cannot generate.
quiz.why: Commodity content is where most AI marketing spend is currently wasted, because answer engines already synthesise that material. Blaming prompt quality is the seductive error: no prompt turns a restatement of page one into new information, and the correct response to AI-abundant content is original research and named expert opinion.

quiz.q: In the human strategy, AI production, human editing workflow, what breaks if you skip each human step?
options: Skip strategy and you produce fluent nonsense; skip editing and you produce fluent averageness.
Skip strategy and output slows down; skip editing and you risk copyright problems.
Skip strategy and the brand voice drifts; skip editing and the volume falls.
Skip strategy and you cannot measure results; skip editing and you breach disclosure rules.
quiz.why: Strategy - what we are saying, to whom, why it beats the alternative - cannot be delegated because a model has no access to your customers or margins. Editing is where the specific claim, the number and the customer quote get added, so skipping it leaves output that is smooth, hedged and indistinguishable from a competitor's.

quiz.q: Your AI-assisted ads are fluent but sound exactly like your competitor's. What is the fix?
options: Switch to a different model, since voice differences come from the model.

Write a context file with ICP, positioning, message hierarchy, five to eight concrete voice rules, real proof assets and forbidden claims, attach it to every task, and prompt for range rather than polish.
Generate many more variants and pick the best one.
Add stronger calls to action and more vivid adjectives to the prompt.
quiz.why: Default output converges on the same smooth, hedged register, and the context file is what converts a generic writer into something that sounds like your company; the proof assets are also what stops it inventing numbers. Generating more variants is tempting but only produces more of the same average, because the missing input is context, not volume.

quiz.q: A draft report contains a compelling market statistic the model supplied, and the deadline is today. What is the standard?
options: Publish it with a hedge such as 'industry estimates suggest', which covers the uncertainty.
Publish it; the model is usually right about widely quoted figures.
Every figure, citation, price and capability claim needs a source before publication, and the byline owns the claim regardless of what produced it.
Ask the model to verify its own statistic and publish if it confirms it.
quiz.why: Models invent statistics, studies, quotes and product features with complete confidence, and one published fabrication can cost more credibility than the content earns in a year. Asking the model to check itself fails the standing rule: AI is reliable at organising information you give it and unreliable at recalling information it was not given.

quiz.q: When does AI use require disclosure?
options: On everything AI touched, including drafts, so the audience can judge for itself.
Where the audience would otherwise feel misled - synthetic people, AI imagery presented as photography, AI voices, testimonials not from real customers - but not for AI as a drafting tool.
Never; it is a tool like a spellchecker and disclosure only invites scepticism.
Only where a specific platform's terms happen to require it.
quiz.why: The line is whether the audience would feel misled, and fabricated endorsements are a legal problem in many jurisdictions rather than merely an ethical one. Disclosing every draft is the over-correction: using AI to draft carries no more obligation than using a spellchecker, though a byline still means that person is accountable for every claim.

cards.front: What do AI's genuine leverage cases have in common?
cards.back: They are high-volume, structured, verifiable, and bounded by production capacity rather than judgment: research synthesis, first drafts, creative variants, ad copy at scale, data and SQL work, feedback clustering, personalisation, campaign QA.

cards.front: State the three-step workflow and what breaks at each end.
cards.back: Human sets strategy, AI produces, human edits with taste. Skip the strategy and you produce fluent nonsense; skip the editing and you produce fluent averageness.

cards.front: What are the five components of a strong marketing prompt?
cards.back: Role and task stated specifically; the ICP with situation, trigger and language; the positioning with differentiator and proof; two or three good examples and one bad with reasons; constraints on length, format, forbidden claims and the action.

cards.front: What goes in a context file?
cards.back: Company and product in three sentences, ICP with trigger and budget reality, positioning and proof, message hierarchy, five to eight concrete voice rules, real proof assets and quotes, forbidden claims, two on-brand examples. Under two pages, versioned.

cards.front: What is the standing rule about what AI can be trusted with?
cards.back: It is reliable at organising information you give it and unreliable at recalling information it was not given. Structure every research use around that boundary and verify the claims that matter.

cards.front: Which skills appreciate as production is commoditised?
cards.back: Taste, judgment, customer understanding from conversations you had yourself, original information, distribution and relationships, and accountability. Prompting is a temporary advantage that erodes as models improve.

elaborate: Draw your own leverage and destruction line for your chosen business: five tasks you will delegate to AI and five you will not, with one sentence of reasoning for each. Then name the single piece of information only your business could publish, and write its headline and the three data points it would contain.

M14 noted that AI made variant production nearly free while your traffic did not multiply by fifty. Explain what that means for how many hypotheses you actually need versus how many variants you can produce, and where those extra variants are better spent.

transfer.scenario: A five-person agency has a marketing lead who spent three days a week writing blog posts. The founder buys an AI writing tool, sets a target of 30 posts a month, and drops the lead's two weekly customer interviews to free up the time. Three months in, organic traffic is up 8 percent, demo requests are flat, the posts read like every competitor's, and one post cited a statistic that does not exist - a prospect noticed and mentioned it on a call.
transfer.prompt: Redesign how that marketing lead spends the week.
transfer.model: Two errors compounded: volume treated as a strategy, and outsourcing the customer contact that made the copy specific. Reinstate the two interviews a week, done by the lead, with AI clustering the transcripts afterwards and pulling verbatim quotes rather than paraphrases. Drop the 30-post target entirely. Build the context file - ICP, positioning, message hierarchy, five to eight voice rules with real never-say items, and real proof assets and quotes, which is what stops the model inventing statistics. Add a quality gate: every factual claim sourced, sounds like us, contains at least one thing only we could have said, and a named human accountable. Then move the freed time to where AI genuinely pays: creative variants for the ad account, an agent-assembled weekly report the lead spends twenty minutes interpreting, and one original asset a quarter built from the agency's own client data.

predict: If you had to judge two go-to-market plans for the same business, guess one thing that would tell you which author has more judgment.

quiz.q: Which of these is a diagnosis rather than a wish?
options: We need more sales, and faster than last year.
We want to be the recognised category leader within eighteen months.
We convert 4 percent of demo requests to paid against a 12 percent category norm, and we have no idea why.
Our marketing budget is too small for the goals we have been given.
quiz.why: A diagnosis names the single most important constraint on growth, stated as a constraint and backed by evidence, and everything downstream should follow from that sentence. The budget complaint is the most tempting wrong answer because it sounds specific and analytical, but it is a wish for more resource rather than a named, evidenced constraint you can act on.

quiz.q: A plan's channel section lists five channels with a paragraph of justification for each and no exclusions. How does it score on the rubric?
options: Weak. Level 1 is 'lists every channel'; a 3 requires two or three channels chosen with roles assigned, expected cost per outcome tested against max CPA, and at least three exclusions justified specifically.
Competent. Reasons were given for each channel, which is what level 2 asks for.
Strong. Five reasoned channels shows breadth of understanding.
It cannot be scored until the budget section is read alongside it.
quiz.why: The rubric's level 2 is two or three channels chosen with reasons, so listing five fails even that bar regardless of how good the paragraphs are. Explicit exclusions - what you are not doing and why - are described as the strongest signal of judgment in the document, and vague dismissal does not count.

quiz.q: Your plan states an £80 AOV, 45 percent gross margin, an average 1.8 purchases per customer over a 24-month horizon, a 3:1 LTV:CAC target, and a 3 percent landing page conversion rate. What is the most you can pay per click?
options: About £1.44, since LTV is £80 x 1.8 = £144, divided by three and multiplied by the conversion rate.
About £21.60, which is what you can afford per customer.
About £0.65: LTV on gross profit is £64.80, max CAC at 3:1 is £21.60, and each click is worth 3 percent of that.
About £2.16, being max CAC divided by ten.
quiz.why: The chain runs AOV to gross profit to LTV at a capped horizon to max CAC to max CPA per funnel step, and £80 x 0.45 x 1.8 is £64.80, so max CAC is £21.60 and a click at 3 percent conversion is worth about £0.65. The £1.44 answer computes LTV on revenue instead of gross profit, which more than doubles what you would bid.

quiz.q: Section 9 asks for an attribution stance and the one incrementality test you run first. Which version belongs in a strong plan?
options: A commitment to build a media mix model within the first 90 days as the source of truth.
Three or four sentences on what you will and will not trust, naming branded search or retargeting as the first holdout.
A commitment to GA4's data-driven model as the source of truth, as the most advanced of its three models.
A statement that once tracking is fixed, attribution will show which channels cause sales.
quiz.why: Branded search or retargeting is usually the right first incrementality test because that is where non-incremental spend hides. Naming GA4's data-driven model is the plausible-sounding trap: GA4 does retain three attribution models, but no attribution model establishes causation, which is the point the stance has to make.

quiz.q: Your experiment backlog's top hypothesis needs 90,000 sessions and you get 4,000 a week. How should the plan handle it?
options: Include only hypotheses you can test to 95 percent confidence, and cut this one from the backlog.
Leave the sample size check out, because it makes the plan look pessimistic to a reader.
ICE-score the hypotheses but leave them unranked, so you stay flexible about what to run.
State the sample size reality check openly and name the alternative method, since a plan that admits it lacks the traffic to A/B test scores higher than one that pretends otherwise.
quiz.why: The rubric's level 3 for experiments is the sample size reality check done and an honest alternative where testing is not possible, and confident vagueness is exactly what experienced readers screen for. Cutting the hypothesis is tempting but wrong: the idea may still be the right thing to do, just not by A/B test.

quiz.q: Which risk entry earns a 3 on the rubric?
options: If CPA on Meta prospecting exceeds £45 for three consecutive weeks with acceptable creative volume, we stop and shift the budget to partnerships.
Rising advertising costs could make acquisition harder over time; we will monitor performance closely.
Competitors may copy our positioning; we will mitigate this by continuing to differentiate.
Platform algorithm changes are a risk, which we mitigate by diversifying across channels.
quiz.why: A 3 requires an observable trip-wire and a stated course change: the specific condition that would make you change the plan. The other three are risks with mitigations, which is level 2 at best, because none of them names a number or a moment at which you would actually do something differently.

cards.front: What is the capstone deliverable, and who is it written for?
cards.back: A six to ten page go-to-market plan for one real business, written for a smart, busy non-marketer: a CEO, investor, client or interviewer. Length is a constraint, not a target.

cards.front: Name the standards a strong plan meets.
cards.back: Decisions rather than options; numbers everywhere they belong, with each assumption labelled measured, benchmarked or guessed; explicit exclusions; uncertainty stated rather than hidden; plain language with no unearned jargon.

cards.front: What makes a diagnosis rather than a wish?
cards.back: One specific evidenced constraint on growth - not 'we need more sales' but '4 percent of demo requests convert against a 12 percent category norm'. Every later section should trace back to it.

cards.front: Which four sections do you protect if you run short of time?
cards.back: Situation and diagnosis, positioning, unit economics, and measurement. A sharp diagnosis, real positioning, honest economics and a measurement stance beat a padded ten pages.

cards.front: What must the unit economics section contain to score a 3?
cards.back: The full chain to max CPA per funnel step, computed on gross profit, with the retention assumption and a capped horizon, the LTV:CAC ratio reasoning, payback addressed, and every assumption labelled.

cards.front: What separates a level-2 risk from a level-3 risk?
cards.back: A trip-wire: the observable condition that would make you change the plan, plus the stated course change. Include at least one external risk and one internal one.

elaborate: Write the diagnosis sentence for your chosen business in one line: the single most important constraint on growth, stated as a constraint with evidence attached. Then take three sections you have already drafted across earlier modules and say honestly, for each, whether it addresses that constraint or is simply in the plan out of habit.

Score your own plan against the twelve-row rubric and be harsh about it. Take your three lowest rows, write one concrete action and a date for each, and name which earlier module you would reread first before attempting the rewrite.

transfer.scenario: You are handed a nine-page go-to-market plan for a £120 per month B2B tool. The ICP section is genuinely good, with a clear trigger and three verbatim customer quotes, and the positioning statement fills the template correctly. The channel section covers SEO, paid search, paid social, LinkedIn organic, podcasts, events and partnerships with a paragraph each, and the budget is stated as 10 percent of forecast revenue. The measurement section lists GA4, HubSpot and Looker Studio, and four generic risks each have a mitigation. The diagnosis reads 'we need to grow faster', and there is no unit economics section at all.
transfer.prompt: Identify the weakest rows and say what you would send back first.
transfer.model: Rows 1, 5, 6 and 8 are ones, and the total lands well under 24, which means this is a description rather than a strategy. Three things go back first. The diagnosis: 'we need to grow faster' is a wish, so name one specific evidenced constraint, then check every section traces to it. The unit economics, which are missing entirely: ACV, gross margin, LTV on gross profit at a capped horizon, max CAC at a stated ratio with the reasoning, payback against the cash position, and max CPA per funnel step worked backwards. The channels: cut seven to two or three, assign creation or capture roles, test expected cost per outcome against max CPA, and justify at least three exclusions specifically. Rebuild the budget objective-and-task, not as a percentage, with answers for minus 20 percent and plus 50 percent. The ICP section is already strong; leave it.
